analysis.title: "Gold Has Become An Inverse Oil Trade": Goldman Explains Why Bullion Ripped As Brent Crashed 20%
key_insights: Goldman's Rich Privorotsky argues gold has become an inverse oil trade. EM central banks that accumulated gold as a reserve asset tapped or stopped buying it when energy bills rose, and as oil falls the funding pressure eases and gold catches a bid. He calls it 'not proven' but more compelling than real rates alone for recent price action.

Brent fell 9% on Wednesday after the Democratic sweep and Trump's 'no immediate plans' for new Iran strikes, for a weekly loss of roughly 20%. Gold rose more than 3%, its biggest daily gain since August, to about $4,130.

Gold fell from a record above $5,600 in January to below $4,000 by Monday, even as Brent reached $124 after the February 28 US/Israel strikes on Iran. The article attributes the decline to forced EM central bank selling.

Turkey sold 58 tons of gold in the two weeks after the war began, about 15% of its inventory, to defend the lira and pay energy bills. Global central banks were net sellers in March for the first time in ten months, and Russia also sold.
Commerzbank's Carsten Fritsch noted in June that the oil-gold correlation had swung to -0.6, versus +0.5 just before the war.

Privorotsky says physical Brent has 'effectively collapsed', with Dated Brent at a discount to prompt futures and the front three weeks in contango. Some argue fair value is below $70. He worries 'we are a bit ahead of ourselves' and flags weekend escalation risk.
Privorotsky says long gold is potentially a more defensible de-escalation trade than short oil, because much of the war premium has already come out of oil.

Goldman's commodities desk (Adam Gillard) says gold is rallying on CTA covering and modest Chinese buying, with no significant macro engagement. China has covered SHFE shorts and is adding modest length.

Gillard says investors built option length twice this year to about 50% of January highs, and price gave up both times on rates and oil. The GS CTA model is close to max short, so the pain trade is likely higher.
GS CTA positioning gauge fell from about +4 in late summer to about -7, the lowest in the two-year history shown.

GLD had its first monthly outflow since June (-$1.8B), nearly reversing September's inflows. Gillard puts the GLD plus iShares holders' local VWAP near $4,400/oz, about 6% above spot, which may cap the first leg of a rally.

Bloomberg's Simon White said last Friday's 3.7% gold liquidation looked like a liquidity-raising move and took gold below fair value for the first time since 2023. Goldman's James McGeoch noted open interest up 1% with longs adding.

World Gold Council data: Q3 central bank buying was 321 tons, up 42% y/y, the fastest pace since 2024, led by China's PBOC and Poland, with 675 tons YTD. Gold ETFs took in a record $31B in Q3, with holdings at an all-time high of 4,256 tons.

Skeptics: Citi's Luis Costa closed a short MXN/ZAR position at a 1.75% loss, citing a challenging short-term gold outlook. Goldman's Australian mining analysts note miners are short oil, since diesel is 1-10% of AISC and remains at the top of guidance ranges, so near-term margin compression is a risk.
Goldman's Hugo Nicolaci cut Genesis Minerals (GMD) to Neutral and Regis Resources (RRL) to Sell. The Aussie sector is pricing in roughly US$3,600/oz versus spot and forwards of about US$4,000+.

The article's view is that de-escalation is the more likely path. It argues the new Democratic majority is expected to reverse spending cuts and deficits will rise, which supports gold as a debasement trade regardless of oil.

Privorotsky says oil is priced for peace before a deal, with physical Brent at a discount and some arguing fair value below $70. Shorting here means betting the peace premium keeps draining after a 20% weekly drop.

tension_points.bull_case: Falling oil eases funding pressure on EM reserve holders, so forced gold selling stops. CTAs are near max short, central banks and ETFs are buying structurally, and gold is below fair value.
tension_points.bear_case: Privorotsky calls the thesis 'not proven'. GLD holders' VWAP near $4,400 may cap the rally, Citi sees a challenging short-term outlook, and a weekend escalation would send Brent up and force EM selling again.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Another weekend escalation in which Brent rips and EM central banks sell gold again.

tension_points.bull_case: Bullion is recovering and the Aussie sector prices only about US$3,600/oz versus spot and forwards of about US$4,000+.
tension_points.bear_case: Miners are short oil. Diesel at the top end of guidance ranges, 1-10% of AISC, compresses near-term margins.
tension_points.what_invalidates: The inverse oil trade only pays off for miners once cheaper fuel shows up in their costs.
